title: A rule of life
hookLine: Benedict wrote a "little rule for beginners," a shape for a whole life (Rule of Benedict, prologue and chapter 73)
tomorrow: Franklin kept a little book full of black dots. what was he marking?

cards: The hermit was Benedict. Pope Gregory the Great tells it. As a young man Benedict walked away from his studies in Rome and lived alone in a cave at Subiaco.
Monks from a nearby monastery, whose abbot had died, begged him to lead them. He warned them his ways wouldn't suit them. They insisted.

Soon his strictness chafed, and they slipped poison into his wine. When he made the sign of the cross over the glass, it shattered. Benedict stood up, told them to find an abbot to their taste, and went back to his cave.

teach.b: Years later he founded his own communities, and wrote them a rule, a regula. Some readers see the shattered glass behind its gentleness. In the prologue he says he hopes to set down nothing harsh, nothing burdensome.
Near the end he calls the whole thing a little rule for beginners. And it opens with a posture: Ausculta, o fili. Listen, my son, and incline the ear of your heart.
Here's today's question: how do you give a whole life a shape?

teach.h: EVERY HOUR HAS A PLACE TO STAND.
teach.b: Benedict's answer, from his Christian faith, is a rule of life: a short, written pattern for the day, prayer at set hours, work, reading, meals and sleep, so that every hour has a place to stand. He even lets it bend.
If anyone has a better way to arrange the psalms, he writes, let them arrange it. Benedictine monks and nuns still live by it.

His prayer hours lean on a psalm: "Seven times a day do I praise thee." A neighbor tradition keeps the day by the clock of prayer too. In Pickthall's Qur'an: "Worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers."
Muslims stop for salat at set times. Here's the honest difference. For Muslims, the prayer times come as God's command to every believer.
Benedict's hours are one abbot's rule for a monastery, which he himself said could be rearranged.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Benedict, praying the hours of the Divine Office together and reading a passage of the Rule each day; Muslims pray salat at set times through the day.

o: a list of punishments for monks who break the law
a ruler used to keep lines straight in a monastery
a short written pattern that gives a day its shape

games.q: Benedict's little rule: tap the pairs.
p: the glass shatters at his blessing

s: Benedict's Rule calls itself a demanding code for spiritual experts
he calls it a little rule for beginners and hopes to set down nothing harsh or burdensome.
Benedict let his communities rearrange the psalms if they found a better way
the Rule says so plainly about the order of the psalms.
a rule of life is a list of punishments
it's a written pattern for the day: prayer, work, reading, meals and sleep.

games.q: a coworker steps out at set times to pray salat. a new hire asks if that's the same as a monk's hours. what's a fair answer?
o: both shape the day with prayer at set times; for Muslims it's God's command to every believer, while Benedict's hours are a monastery's rule.
yes, it's exactly the same practice under different names.
no, the two have nothing at all in common.
games.why: the Qur'an says worship at fixed hours is enjoined on the believers; Benedict wrote hours for monks and let them be rearranged. shared, and honestly different.

practice: Sit and tilt your head a little, the way you lean in to hear a friend in a loud room. That's the posture Benedict's Rule begins with: incline the ear of your heart. Stay there for two minutes, listening to whatever is here.

wordCard.voice: Regula: Latin for a rule. Benedict's is a little rule for beginners, a gentle shape for a whole day.

orig.note: Latin: a rule. Benedict calls his a little rule for beginners.

carryVoice: The line to keep: a little rule, nothing harsh, nothing burdensome, written for beginners. See you tomorrow.
